title: Worldbuilding
author: Livid_Shallot5701
selftext:
A question for everyone building "their own world".

How much lore do you produce for your games? for me its a rabid hole and every new event, nation, person, etc. i invent, it could spark other 10 more things, and those could each spawn 10 more. 

so how much did you flesh outr your lore (especially rpg or mmo games) and how much time did you invest in lore and world?

thanks guys :D

comments.author: Kingnorik
comments.body: I have a ton of ideas mostly written in Excel files that I'm working into games. Some are 10+ years old.

comments.author: Ragnarocket
comments.body:
For me this is usually something I try to figure out early on. Not every little detail as that would be too much at the start - but the general rules for how the world need to work need to exist at the start. You need to understand how systems might work in terms of "your world". If you have magic, how does it work? You don't need too much nuance at this point but you should be able to answer some high level questions. 

As you get more into the nitty gritty of your story, then start figuring out the NPCs, the places, the "whys" of it all. Is there a city in a specific place? Why is it there, how does it make sense in the world...and try not to bog yourself down with all sorts of needless side tangents. Once you have your core set up you can branch out to add flavor to your world but you should focus on the big stuff first.

comments.author: ItsDumi
comments.body:
Honestly, I started by building all the system first, no content unless it was needed for testing. Now, I'm done with my core engine and I've just been thinking about story, modeling and designing. It's been fun because, like you said, it's endless. And those are the skills I ACTUALLY have, building my engine was just an unfortunate need for my vision.

I have an mvp in mind though, so while I'm designing content I'm also polishing until it's good enough for playtesting. It's easy to get lost in the sauce so having a clear game loop and deliverable is very important imo

comments.author: cheyumaama
comments.body: You can have infinite lore. It's just delivery that's important. The lore should spin around the gameplay so that you have enough gameplay for a game release. Then when you have enough, you can release the game as part 1 or chapter 1 and then continue the lore in future chapters when you invent more gameplay with respect to the lore that would revolve around it

replies.body: good point. in a typical fantasy world where the player can spawn anywhere they like on the planet, how  would you go around giving them lore? i mean if they see an elf they dont needto know their history to know "this one is probably acting a little elfish and esoteric" etc. so, nothing and only when they talk to people or visit places they learn "what" they are seeing and why someone hates someone else and why the city looks so strange etc. ? sounds organic to me witha little risk of the "start" being "too crazy" if they go next to the main city hub warzone or smth

replies.author: cheyumaama
replies.body: You need to have your gameplay ready first and then spin lore around that. The first question you need to answer is "Where is the player? i.e. what planet/city/village/setting, etc." and secondly, "why is the player there?". When you have answered these two questions, you can create the world and start the gameplay part of just getting your player to walk around and run around in the setting that you have created. Next, as you move around it, you will get further ideas on what the setting needs - to look alive and thriving, for eg: what kind of people/creatures inhabit that setting, what does the environment look like and so on. Once you build that, the next steps to add will naturally flow into your mind. For eg: If he's now in a village of elves in an elven kingdom, what does he do there? Is he an elf himself? Does he go to some elf school? Does he work there? Does he have a family, etc. You can craft gameplay around any of these variable situations and build out your world step by step.

replies.author: Livid_Shallot5701
replies.body: you misunderstood. my players can chose any place on the planet surface, be it capital city or desert, to start. its kind of like a start in rimworld.

replies.author: cheyumaama
replies.body: Ah I see...Then whatever place they choose must be built out completely. If it follows a story, then starting at any place should eventually lead to the same convergence point regardless of where a player starts from. Giving the players any place to start from actually makes your work upfront harder because you need to have built out multiple levels in multiple different settings each with their own unique dynamic before you can hope to ship the game, so doing the story as chapters or parts cannot work in this case

replies.author: Livid_Shallot5701
replies.body:
thats true. but i dont have a huge main story, its more like a story generator. you know rimworld, battle brothers, mount and blade, etc.? you set your starting settings and then have an open living world where you can "do what you want" in the context of the game. so its not realy a strict story but "arcing world event story" that i have, like demons invading the whole world. but every place, biome, country still needs his lore. even more so i dare say as its the only story you "get" ingame. there is no fix storyline telling you whats happening but you have to experience it or get it from townspeople or taverns or traveling etc. 

i never did this before, only small linear rpgs so im a bit unsure how im going about it and how deep i need to go at which point in development.

comments.author: ErickWickings
comments.body:
With lore, and world building, I think you ave to put yourself in the player's shoes... You love this world and you want to build more of it because it matters to you / you find it fascinating / could spend hours in it.... But would a player?  
With AI, generating the next story, the nth faction, etc. costs very little.... But players attention will be a lot more "expensive" for you to capture... So I'd say, make sure you have the right stuff where it's needed, before going deeper.... Also the more you create, the more difficult I find it to track everything and make sure that everything stays coherent especially necause pieces of lore should interact with one another rather than live in their own silos... Just my 2 cents...
